transcript: okay so um today we're gonna continue with uh operating systems right so last class we covered process scheduling and today we're doing memory management so uh the first thing to understand is that every process thinks it has the entire memory to itself right that's the whole point of virtual memory so um each process has its own virtual address space and the OS maps that to physical memory using something called a page table so uh a page table is basically a data structure that maps virtual page numbers to physical frame numbers okay so when a process tries to access a memory address the CPU looks up the page table translates the virtual address to a physical address and then accesses that physical location so uh the problem is page tables can be huge right if you have a 32 bit address space with 4 kilobyte pages you have like a million entries in the page table so that's a lot of memory just for the page table itself so um to solve this we use multi level page tables where instead of one big table we have a hierarchy of tables so only the parts of the address space that are actually being used have page table entries allocated so uh any questions on that before I move on to TLBs

so today's lecture is on neural networks specifically backpropagation which is honestly one of the most important algorithms in all of machine learning so um the whole point of backpropagation is to compute gradients efficiently so we can update the weights of the network during training so let me first remind you of the forward pass right so in the forward pass we take our input and we pass it through each layer computing activations until we get to the output and compute the loss so the loss tells us how wrong our predictions are and we want to minimize it so backpropagation is basically the reverse pass where we go from the output back to the input computing gradients along the way using the chain rule from calculus so the chain rule says that if you have a composition of functions the derivative of the whole thing is the product of the derivatives of each part so um in a neural network each layer is like a function and we apply the chain rule repeatedly going backwards through the network to get the gradient of the loss with respect to each weight so those gradients then tell us which direction to move each weight to reduce the loss and that's gradient descent so the combination of backprop to compute gradients and gradient descent to update weights is basically how all neural networks are trained today so uh make sure you understand the chain rule because I guarantee it will be on the exam

so um today we're covering database normalization which is super important for the DBMS exam next week so uh normalization is basically the process of organizing a relational database to reduce redundancy and improve data integrity so we have different normal forms right first normal form second normal form third normal form and BCNF so let's start with first normal form so a table is in first normal form if every column contains atomic values meaning no repeating groups no arrays no nested tables so for example if you have a student table and you have a column called phone numbers with multiple phone numbers in one cell that violates first normal form so you need to break that out into a separate table so second normal form adds the requirement that every non-key attribute must be fully functionally dependent on the primary key so this only applies to tables with composite keys so if you have a table with a composite key and one of the non-key columns only depends on part of the key that's a partial dependency and you need to remove it so third normal form removes transitive dependencies so if column A determines column B and column B determines column C then column C transitively depends on A and that should be moved to a separate table so the way I remember it is Codd's definition every non-key attribute must depend on the key the whole key and nothing but the key so uh let's do some examples to make this concrete

so uh picking up from where we left off last time we were talking about sorting algorithms and today we're going to cover merge sort and quicksort and compare them so um merge sort is a divide and conquer algorithm so the idea is you split the array in half recursively sort each half and then merge the two sorted halves together so the merge step is the key part you have two sorted arrays and you want to combine them into one sorted array so you compare the first elements of each array take the smaller one add it to your result and repeat until one array is empty then append the remaining elements so the time complexity of merge sort is O n log n in all cases best case worst case and average case because we always split in half and the merge takes linear time so uh the space complexity is O n because we need auxiliary space for the merge step now quicksort is also divide and conquer but it works differently so you choose a pivot element partition the array so all elements less than the pivot come before it and all elements greater come after it and then recursively sort the two partitions so the time complexity of quicksort is O n log n on average but O n squared in the worst case which happens when you always pick the smallest or largest element as the pivot like if the array is already sorted and you always pick the first element so uh in practice quicksort is usually faster than merge sort because it has better cache performance even though worst case is worse so most standard library sort implementations use introsort which is a hybrid of quicksort heapsort and insertion sort

so today I want to talk about computer networks specifically the OSI model and TCP IP model because these come up constantly in interviews and exams so um the OSI model has seven layers physical data link network transport session presentation and application so a lot of people use the mnemonic Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away or some variation to remember them so the physical layer is the actual hardware bits on a wire the data link layer handles node to node communication and error detection think Ethernet and MAC addresses the network layer handles routing between networks that's where IP lives the transport layer provides end to end communication and that's TCP and UDP the session layer manages sessions between applications the presentation layer handles data formatting and encryption and the application layer is where user facing protocols live like HTTP FTP SMTP so um in practice the TCP IP model is what's actually implemented and it collapses some of these layers so it has four layers network access internet transport and application so the network access layer combines physical and data link the internet layer is IP the transport layer is TCP UDP and the application layer covers session presentation and application from OSI so the reason we still teach OSI is that it's a useful conceptual framework for understanding where different protocols operate and for troubleshooting network issues so if there's a connectivity problem you can systematically go through each layer to isolate the issue

so uh today's topic is object oriented programming specifically inheritance and polymorphism which are two of the four pillars of OOP so um let's start with inheritance so inheritance is a mechanism where a child class derives properties and behaviors from a parent class so the idea is code reuse right instead of writing the same code in multiple classes you write it once in the parent class and all child classes inherit it so for example if you have an Animal class with attributes like name and age and methods like eat and sleep then you can have child classes like Dog and Cat that inherit those attributes and methods and then add their own specific ones like Dog has a bark method and Cat has a purr method so um in Python you do this by passing the parent class name in the class definition so class Dog colon Animal and then inside the Dog class you only define what's different or additional so now polymorphism is related to inheritance it means different classes can be treated as instances of the same parent class so you can have a list of Animal objects some of which are Dogs and some are Cats and you can call the same method on all of them and each one will behave according to its own implementation so this is called method overriding where the child class provides its own implementation of a method that's already defined in the parent class so um the classic example is a shape class with an area method and then circle rectangle triangle all override the area method with their own formula so this makes your code much more flexible and extensible

so um today we're doing trees specifically binary search trees and the operations on them so a binary search tree is a binary tree where for every node all values in the left subtree are less than the node's value and all values in the right subtree are greater so this property is what makes search efficient so let's talk about the search operation so to search for a value you start at the root if the value equals the root you found it if it's less you go left if it's greater you go right and you repeat until you find it or reach a null so the time complexity is O h where h is the height of the tree so in the best case the tree is balanced and h is log n so search is O log n but in the worst case the tree is completely unbalanced like if you insert elements in sorted order you just get a linked list and h is n so search is O n so insertion works similarly you find the correct position by following the BST property and insert the node there so deletion is the tricky one there are three cases if the node has no children you just remove it if it has one child you replace the node with that child and if it has two children you find the inorder successor which is the smallest value in the right subtree replace the node's value with that and then delete the inorder successor so um to avoid the worst case of unbalanced trees we use self balancing BSTs like AVL trees and red black trees which maintain balance automatically through rotations but we'll cover those next class

so today we're gonna look at dynamic programming which honestly trips up a lot of students but once you get the intuition it's really powerful so um dynamic programming is basically about breaking a problem into overlapping subproblems solving each subproblem once and storing the results so you don't recompute them so the two key properties a problem needs for DP to apply are optimal substructure meaning the optimal solution to the problem contains optimal solutions to subproblems and overlapping subproblems meaning the same subproblems come up repeatedly so the classic example everyone starts with is Fibonacci right so if you just implement Fibonacci recursively you recompute the same values over and over so fib of 5 calls fib of 4 and fib of 3 and fib of 4 calls fib of 3 and fib of 2 so fib of 3 gets computed multiple times so with memoization you store the result of fib of 3 the first time you compute it and just look it up after that so the time complexity goes from exponential to linear so there are two approaches top down which is recursion with memoization and bottom up which is iterative and builds up from the smallest subproblems so for Fibonacci bottom up you start with fib of 0 equals 0 fib of 1 equals 1 and then compute fib of 2 fib of 3 and so on using previously computed values so uh the harder part is recognizing when a problem can be solved with DP and formulating the recurrence relation and we'll practice that with several problems today starting with the knapsack problem

so uh the topic today is graph algorithms and specifically we're looking at breadth first search and depth first search so these are the two fundamental ways to traverse a graph and they have really different properties and use cases so um a graph is just a set of nodes and edges connecting them and the edges can be directed or undirected and weighted or unweighted so BFS breadth first search starts at a source node and explores all neighbors at the current depth before going deeper so you use a queue data structure and you visit nodes level by level so the first level is the source node the second level is all nodes directly connected to the source the third level is all nodes connected to those and so on so BFS is great for finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs because it explores nodes in order of their distance from the source so the first time you reach a node in BFS is guaranteed to be via the shortest path so uh time complexity is O V plus E where V is the number of vertices and E is the number of edges because you visit each vertex and edge once so DFS depth first search goes as deep as possible before backtracking so you use a stack either explicitly or through recursion so DFS is useful for detecting cycles topological sorting finding connected components and solving maze problems so uh the time complexity is also O V plus E so they're the same asymptotically but their behavior is very different and choosing the right one depends on the problem so let's code up both and then look at some problems

so today we're covering the last topic before the end sem exam which is compiler design specifically the phases of a compiler so um a compiler takes source code as input and produces machine code as output and it does this through several phases so the first phase is lexical analysis or scanning so the scanner reads the source code character by character and groups them into tokens so tokens are the meaningful units like keywords identifiers operators literals and punctuation so for example if you have int x equals 5 the tokens are int which is a keyword x which is an identifier equals which is an operator and 5 which is an integer literal so uh the second phase is syntax analysis or parsing so the parser takes the token stream and checks if it follows the grammar of the language and builds a parse tree or abstract syntax tree so the grammar is usually specified as a context free grammar using BNF notation so if there's a syntax error the parser reports it here so the third phase is semantic analysis where we check for things the grammar can't catch like type mismatches using an undeclared variable or calling a function with the wrong number of arguments so the symbol table is heavily used in this phase to track identifiers and their types so the fourth phase is intermediate code generation where we translate the AST into an intermediate representation that's easier to optimize and translate to machine code so three address code is a common IR so then we have optimization passes and finally code generation which produces the target machine code so uh the exam will definitely have questions on first and second phases so make sure you can do lexical analysis by hand and trace through a simple parse
